name: अर्जुनविषादयोग
teaching: Before any teaching can begin, something must break. Arjuna — the finest warrior alive — looks at what his duty actually costs and collapses. The Gita honours his collapse: despair, seen clearly, is the doorway to inquiry. The tradition honors this collapse by calling the chapter a yoga: despair, fully felt and honestly spoken, is the first spiritual posture. Nothing true can be taught to a self still pretending it is fine.
questions: Where in your life are you certain you are right, the way Duryodhana is certain?
Arjuna's reasons for not acting sound noble. When have your own noblest-sounding reasons hidden fear?
What would it take for you to set down your bow — to admit, fully, 'I do not know what to do'?

verses.speaker: धृतराष्ट्र उवाच
verses.devanagari:
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय॥
verses.transliteration:
dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ
māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata sañjaya
verses.essence: A blind king asks what happened on the field where dharma itself was at stake.
verses.translation: What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together eager for battle on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya.

anvaya.parts: धर्म (righteousness) + क्षेत्र (field): the field of dharma

anvaya.base: कुरुक्षेत्र · the field of the Kurus
anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kuru clan) + क्षेत्र (field): the field of the Kurus

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative plural (who have assembled)

anvaya.base: युयुत्सु · wishing to fight (from √युध् · to fight)
anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative plural (desiderative: wanting to fight)
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural
verb, imperfect (past), 3rd person plural, middle voice

anvaya.base: सञ्जय · Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and narrator

verses.explanation: The Gita opens not with Krishna but with Dhritarashtra's anxiety. The old king calls the field 'dharma-kshetra' — the field where dharma is upheld — yet in the same breath divides its people into 'mine' (māmakāḥ) and 'the Pandavas', as if his nephews were not also his own. That one possessive word is the seed of the whole war: the mind that splits the world into mine and not-mine is the mind that makes battlefields. Readers often note that the Gita's first word is dharma and its very last word (18.78) is mama, 'mine' — the whole teaching set between righteousness and possessiveness. Everything Krishna will teach is, in the end, an answer to māmakāḥ.
verses.connection: The question that frames all 700 verses: everything that follows is Sanjaya's answer to this anxious 'what did they do?'
verses.reflection: Before reading on, name your own field — the place where what you do this week will count.
verses.background: In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra turns to his minister Sanjaya, whom Vyasa has granted sight of the distant battlefield. The armies of his sons and of his nephews, the Pandavas, have gathered at Kurukshetra, and the king opens the poem with his question.
verses.hook: What does the blind king really want to know about the battlefield?

refs.note: Calls Kurukshetra the sacrificial arena of the gods, which is why the field was seen as holy ground that nourished dharma.

views.text: Offers an inner reading: the field is the human body, field of the senses (kurus); the 'mine' party are intentions born of ignorance, the Pandavas intentions born of pure knowledge. A mamaka is one who keeps saying 'mine'.

Frames the whole Gita here: the compassionate Lord rescued Arjuna, whose discernment was lost in grief and delusion, by the raft of his teaching, which Vyasa set in seven hundred verses; this verse begins the story that leads to that dialogue.
Explains dharmakshetra as the place that protects dharma, and Sanjaya as one who has conquered likes and dislikes and so can report impartially.
The blind king's question betrays guilt and fear: he worries the holy field might awaken his sons' conscience and lead them to make peace, when he secretly wants the war to happen.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा ।
आचार्यमुपसंगम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्॥
verses.transliteration:
dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṃ vyūḍhaṃ duryodhanastadā
ācāryamupasaṃgamya rājā vacanamabravīt
verses.essence: Seeing the Pandava army arrayed, Duryodhana goes straight to his teacher.
verses.translation: Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle-array, King Duryodhana then approached his teacher (Drona) and spoke these words.

anvaya.form: indeclinable (marks a turn in the story)

anvaya.parts: पाण्डव (the Pandavas) + अनीक (army): the army of the Pandavas

anvaya.base: उप-सम्-√गम् · to go up to, approach

verses.explanation: Sanjaya's report begins with Duryodhana — and with a tell. The king, leader of the larger army, sees the enemy formation and immediately needs to talk. He goes to Drona, his teacher, not to consult strategy but to manage his own unease. Power that is secure does not narrate itself.
verses.connection: Sanjaya begins answering the king's question — with the king's own son's fear.
verses.reflection: Watch how you, too, run to an authority when a rival looks stronger than expected.
verses.background: Sanjaya begins his report to the blind king. On the field the two armies stand drawn up, and the Kaurava prince Duryodhana, having looked over the Pandava formation, goes to Drona, the teacher who trained the princes of both sides, to speak with him.
verses.hook: What does Duryodhana do first when he sees the Pandava army arrayed?

refs.note: Portrays Duryodhana as proud, cruel and hostile to the Pandavas since childhood, the background to his anxious approach to Drona.

views.text: Reads the whole opening speech (1.2-1.11) as a sign of inner defeat: having seen the Pandava forces under Bhima, Duryodhana judged them adequate and his own inadequate, and was grief-stricken within.
Duryodhana goes to his teacher under a show of respect, but the size of the Pandava army has shaken him, and he is really seeking to calm his own nerves.

verses.devanagari:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम् ।
व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता॥
verses.transliteration:
paśyaitāṃ pāṇḍuputrāṇāmācārya mahatīṃ camūm
vyūḍhāṃ drupadaputreṇa tava śiṣyeṇa dhīmatā
verses.essence: Look, teacher: your own brilliant student has arrayed this army against us.
verses.translation: Behold, O Teacher! this mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.

anvaya.parts: पाण्डु (Pandu) + पुत्र (son): sons of Pandu
द्रुपद (Drupada) + पुत्र (son): Drupada's son

verses.explanation: Duryodhana's first sentence is a barb dressed as a report: the enemy formation was designed by Dhrishtadyumna — Drona's own student, born from a sacrifice performed to kill Drona. 'Your clever disciple' is meant to wound and to bind: he is reminding the teacher of his failure, and testing his loyalty before the first arrow flies.
verses.connection: The 'words' announced in the previous verse begin — and they begin with manipulation.
verses.reflection: Notice when you dress a barb as a plain report, reminding someone of an old mistake; say the plain thing instead, or nothing.
verses.background: Duryodhana's words to Drona, which run through 1.11, begin here. He points his teacher to the Pandava host and to the man who has marshalled it, Drupada's son Dhrishtadyumna, once Drona's own pupil.
verses.hook: Why does Duryodhana point out who arranged the enemy army?

views.text: Marks this as the start of Duryodhana's nine-verse speech (1.3-1.11) and names the son of Drupada as Dhrishtadyumna, the arranger of the Pandava array.
By naming Dhrishtadyumna, Drona's own pupil born to kill him, Duryodhana slyly warns his teacher not to go easy on former students now that they stand as enemies.

verses.devanagari:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि ।
युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः॥
verses.transliteration:
atra śūrā maheṣvāsā bhīmārjunasamā yudhi
yuyudhāno virāṭaśca drupadaśca mahārathaḥ
verses.essence: Duryodhana counts the enemy first: heroes equal to Bhima and Arjuna.
verses.translation: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yoyudhana (Satyaki), Virata and Drupada, of the great car (mighty warriors).

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + इष्वास (bow, 'arrow-thrower'): those whose bows are great

anvaya.base: भीमार्जुनसम · equal to Bhima and Arjuna
anvaya.parts: भीम (Bhima) + अर्जुन (Arjuna) + सम (equal): equal to Bhima and Arjuna

anvaya.base: युयुधान · Yuyudhana, another name of Satyaki
विराट · Virata, king of the Matsyas
द्रुपद · Drupada, king of the Panchalas

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + रथ (chariot): one with a great chariot, a top-rank warrior

verses.explanation: Asked nothing, Duryodhana begins listing his enemies — by name, with their ranks. Notice whose army he counts first. A confident commander surveys his own strength; an anxious one cannot stop looking at the other side. The list itself is the confession.
verses.connection: The speech to Drona continues: before naming one ally, he names the threats.
verses.reflection: Notice where your attention goes first under pressure today: to what you have, or to what stands against you.
verses.background: Still addressing Drona, Duryodhana moves from the Pandava army as a whole to the champions in it. This verse carries the first names of his roll-call: Satyaki, Virata and Drupada, great chariot-fighters on the other side.
verses.hook: Which great warriors does Duryodhana see standing with the Pandavas?

views.text: Explains iṣvāsa as 'that by which arrows are thrown', the bow, so maheṣvāsa means one with a great bow; Bhima and Arjuna are named as the yardstick because they are the best-known fighters on that side.
Notes the technical sense of mahāratha: a warrior skilled in the science of war who can fight ten thousand archers alone.
Fear makes the Pandava army look larger than it is to Duryodhana, so he begins anxiously listing their mighty chariot-warriors, each a match for Bhima and Arjuna.

verses.devanagari:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान् ।
पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुंगवः॥
verses.transliteration:
dhṛṣṭaketuścekitānaḥ kāśirājaśca vīryavān
purujitkuntibhojaśca śaibyaśca narapuṃgavaḥ
verses.essence: The count of enemy heroes continues — kings, each one a bull among men.
verses.translation: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana and the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit and Kuntibhoja and Saibya, the best men.

anvaya.base: धृष्टकेतु · Dhrishtaketu, king of the Chedis

anvaya.parts: काशि (Kashi) + राज (king): king of Kashi
नर (man) + पुङ्गव (bull): a bull among men, the best of men

verses.explanation: The roll-call goes on, and every name is a king — many of them kin, like Kuntibhoja and Purujit of Kunti's own family. These are men Duryodhana has known all his life, now standing with the other side. The war he engineered has gathered his whole world onto the opposite bank.
verses.connection: The enemy count from the previous verse continues, growing heavier.
verses.reflection: Even your opposition is made of individuals with histories — try seeing one of them whole today.
verses.background: Duryodhana's roll-call of the Pandava champions continues, still spoken to Drona. This verse carries the second group: allied kings such as Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Shaibya.
verses.hook: Which kings does Duryodhana name next among the Pandava allies?

views.text: Treats the verse as a plain list, adding only that Chekitana is a king and that narapuṅgava, 'bull among men', means the best of men and describes Shaibya.
Duryodhana's list of enemy heroes keeps growing because his anxiety magnifies the strength he sees against him.

verses.devanagari:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान् ।
सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः॥
verses.transliteration:
yudhāmanyuśca vikrānta uttamaujāśca vīryavān
saubhadro draupadeyāśca sarva eva mahārathāḥ
verses.essence: ...and the young ones too: Abhimanyu, Draupadi's five sons — all great warriors.
verses.translation: The strong Yodhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of great chariots (great heroes).

anvaya.base: वि-√क्रम् · to stride forth, be bold
anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: उत्तम (highest) + ओजस् (strength): one of supreme strength
महा (great) + रथ (chariot): top-rank warriors

verses.explanation: The list ends with the children — Abhimanyu, barely sixteen, and Draupadi's five young sons — and Duryodhana grants even them a top military rank, mahārathāḥ. He is not flattering them; he is counting them as threats. War has a way of erasing the line between a boy and a target, and this verse quietly records the erasure.
verses.connection: The enemy roster closes — having descended from veterans to teenagers.
verses.reflection: Notice if you are counting someone young or new only as a rival; for one minute, see how young they are first.
verses.background: The last part of Duryodhana's count of enemy warriors. After the allied kings come Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, then the youngest generation of the Pandava camp: Arjuna's son Abhimanyu and the five sons of Draupadi.
verses.hook: Who are the younger warriors Duryodhana counts on the Pandava side?

views.text: Identifies Saubhadra as Abhimanyu and the Draupadeyas as Prativindhya and his brothers, the five sons born to Draupadi from the five Pandavas, then quotes the scale of ranks: mahāratha fights ten thousand, atiratha countless, ratha one, ardharatha fewer.
Even the youngest fighters on the Pandava side appear to the frightened Duryodhana as great chariot-warriors he had never expected to face.

verses.devanagari:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम ।
नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते॥
verses.transliteration:
asmākaṃ tu viśiṣṭā ye tānnibodha dvijottama
nāyakā mama sainyasya saṃjñārthaṃ tānbravīmi te
verses.essence: Now, for reassurance, Duryodhana turns to naming his own commanders.
verses.translation: Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to thee for thy information.

anvaya.parts: द्विज (twice-born, brahmin) + उत्तम (best): best among brahmins

anvaya.base: संज्ञार्थ · for the sake of knowing
anvaya.form: indeclinable (accusative used as adverb: for the purpose of)
anvaya.parts: संज्ञा (knowledge, notice) + अर्थ (purpose): for the purpose of notice

verses.explanation: Only now — 'for your information', as if Drona did not know his own colleagues — does Duryodhana turn to his side. The phrase is filler; the act is self-soothing. He addresses Drona as 'best of the twice-born', honouring the brahmin in the man he just needled, sweetening after the sting. Watch how anxiety alternates flattery and pressure.
verses.connection: Having counted the threats, he now needs to hear his own strength out loud.
verses.reflection: Now turn the survey around: who actually stands on your side? Count them slowly, with gratitude.
verses.background: Having listed the Pandava champions, Duryodhana turns, still speaking to Drona, to his own side. He addresses the teacher as the best of the twice-born, that is, of Brahmins, and announces a second list.
verses.hook: Why does Duryodhana turn to naming the commanders of his own army?

views.text: Glosses saṃjñārtham as 'for full and correct knowledge' and nāyakāḥ as 'those who lead', treating the line as a straightforward briefing.
Calling Drona 'best of the twice-born' is a veiled taunt about his loyalty; Duryodhana then lists his own generals to cover the insult and lift everyone's morale.

verses.devanagari:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः ।
अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च॥
verses.transliteration:
bhavānbhīṣmaśca karṇaśca kṛpaśca samitiñjayaḥ
aśvatthāmā vikarṇaśca saumadattistathaiva ca
verses.essence: Yourself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashvatthama — the irreplaceable men.
verses.translation: Thyself and Bhishma, and Karna and also Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and also Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta.

anvaya.base: समितिञ्जय · winner of battles (√जि · to conquer)
anvaya.parts: समिति (battle) + जय (conquering): one who conquers in battle

anvaya.base: विकर्ण · Vikarna, a son of Dhritarashtra

verses.explanation: The home roster is shorter and stranger than the enemy's. Bhishma and Drona love the Pandavas they must now fight; Karna has sworn not to fight while Bhishma commands; Vikarna once defended Draupadi against Duryodhana himself in open court. Duryodhana's greatest warriors are men whose hearts are partly on the other side — and he knows it.
verses.connection: The list promised in 1.7 arrives, and it opens with Drona himself and Bhishma, elders who are bound by affection to the other side too.
verses.reflection: Your strongest allies may serve from divided hearts, like Bhishma; love them without testing them.
verses.background: Duryodhana gives the names he has just promised. This verse carries the named commanders of the Kaurava army, beginning with Drona himself and Bhishma; the list closes in the next verse.
verses.hook: Which great warriors lead the Kaurava army?

views.text: Identifies 'your honour' as Drona, explains samitiñjaya as one who conquers in battle (said of Kripa), and names Saumadatti as Bhurishravas, son of Somadatta.

verses.devanagari:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः ।
नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः॥
verses.transliteration:
anye ca bahavaḥ śūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ
nānāśastrapraharaṇāḥ sarve yuddhaviśāradāḥ
verses.essence: And many more heroes, ready to give up their lives — for my sake.
verses.translation: And also many other heroes who are ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, locative singular (for the sake of)
anvaya.parts: मद् (me) + अर्थ (purpose): for my sake

anvaya.meaning: ready to give up their lives
anvaya.base: त्यक्तजीवित · one who has given up life
anvaya.parts: त्यक्त (given up) + जीवित (life): those who have given up life

anvaya.meaning: armed with many kinds of weapons
anvaya.parts: नाना (various) + शस्त्र (weapon) + प्रहरण (means of striking): those whose striking tools are many weapons
युद्ध (battle) + विशारद (expert): experts in battle

verses.explanation: Madarthe — 'for my sake'. Duryodhana says it plainly: thousands will die not for dharma, not for the kingdom, but for him. He intends it as a boast of loyalty, and it lands as the moral ledger of the war. Where Arjuna will soon be paralysed by what others may lose, Duryodhana counts those losses as his assets.
verses.connection: The roster widens from named commanders to the nameless many — all filed under 'mine'.
verses.reflection: Many give their lives to your causes in small unseen installments — notice one such person today.
verses.background: After the named Kaurava commanders, Duryodhana ends his list with the rest of his army: the many unnamed warriors, each with his own weapons, who have come to Kurukshetra to fight on his side.
verses.hook: Who else stands ready to fight and die for Duryodhana?

views.text: Takes tyaktajīvitāḥ as 'resolved to give up life for my purpose' rather than already dead, and nānāśastrapraharaṇāḥ as men whose means of striking are many kinds of weapons.

verses.devanagari:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम् ।
पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
aparyāptaṃ tadasmākaṃ balaṃ bhīṣmābhirakṣitam
paryāptaṃ tvidameteṣāṃ balaṃ bhīmābhirakṣitam
verses.essence: Our army, guarded by Bhishma, is it boundless or not enough? Theirs, guarded by Bhima, seems enough.
verses.translation: This army of ours marshalled by Bhishma is insufficient, whereas that army of theirs marshalled by Bhima is sufficient.

anvaya.parts: भीष्म (Bhishma) + अभिरक्षित (protected): protected by Bhishma

anvaya.base: परि-√आप् · to reach fully: adequate / limited

anvaya.parts: भीम (Bhima) + अभिरक्षित (protected): protected by Bhima

verses.explanation: The verse pivots on one ambiguous word. Aparyāptam can mean 'unlimited' — our army is vast — or 'insufficient' — our army, for all its size, is not enough. The tradition has argued for centuries, and the ambiguity is the truth: Duryodhana himself does not know which he believes. He has eleven divisions to the Pandavas' seven, guarded by the unkillable Bhishma, and still he compares.
verses.connection: The two rosters are weighed against each other — and the scale trembles in his own hand.
verses.reflection: When you call your resources limitless, pause: is that confidence speaking, or the fear underneath it?
verses.background: Both rosters spoken, Duryodhana draws his conclusion for Drona, setting his own host, guarded by Bhishma, beside the Pandava host, guarded by Bhima. Śrīdhara traces his doubt to Bhishma's affection for both sides.
verses.hook: How does Duryodhana compare the strength of the two armies?

views.text: Keeps both senses open: the Bhima-guarded army is either impossible for us to destroy or trivial beside ours, and the Bhishma-guarded army is either destructible by them or too much for them.
Reads aparyāptam as 'insufficient': our army seems unable to fight them because Bhishma is partial to both sides, while theirs seems adequate because Bhima is wholly for one side.
Simply records that commentators differ: Sridhara takes aparyāptam as 'insufficient', Anandagiri as 'unlimited'.
Duryodhana's boast that Bhishma makes his army unlimited shows the vanity that comes before a fall, while Bhishma himself fights half-heartedly, knowing dharma and Krishna stand with the Pandavas.

verses.devanagari:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः ।
भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि॥
verses.transliteration:
ayaneṣu ca sarveṣu yathābhāgamavasthitāḥ
bhīṣmamevābhirakṣantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi
verses.essence: Therefore: all of you, at every post — protect Bhishma above all.
verses.translation: "Therefore do ye all, stationed in your respective positions, in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone."

anvaya.meaning: at the entry points, in the ranks
anvaya.base: अयन · path, way; position in the array

anvaya.parts: यथा (according to) + भाग (share, division): according to division

verses.explanation: The order that ends the speech gives the speaker away: the entire army is instructed to protect its own supreme commander. Strategically there is a kernel of sense — while Bhishma fights at the front, he must not be struck from behind or the flank. Psychologically it is plain: Duryodhana's confidence hangs on one old man, and he has just said so out loud.
verses.connection: The wavering of 1.10 hardens into an order — defend the one pillar everything rests on.
verses.reflection: Notice when worry makes you order everyone to guard one thing; ask whether that thing needs it, or your fear does.
verses.background: From weighing the armies Duryodhana turns to orders. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as what the commanders must therefore do: hold their places at the entrances of the formation, since the life of the Kaurava cause rests on Bhishma's strength.
verses.hook: What order does Duryodhana give his generals before the battle?

views.text: Takes ayana as the entry routes of the battle array; each man keeps his own ground and screens Bhishma so no one strikes him from behind, because, he notes, 'our life rests on Bhishma's strength'.

verses.devanagari:
तस्य सञ्जनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः ।
सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान्॥
verses.transliteration:
tasya sañjanayanharṣaṃ kuruvṛddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ
siṃhanādaṃ vinadyoccaiḥ śaṅkhaṃ dadhmau pratāpavān
verses.essence: To cheer him, old Bhishma roars like a lion and blows his conch.
verses.translation: His glorious grandsire (Bhishma), the oldest of the Kauravas, in order to cheer Duryodhana, now roared like a lion, and blew his conch.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while causing)

anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kurus) + वृद्ध (old, elder): the elder of the Kurus
सिंह (lion) + नाद (roar): a lion's roar

verses.explanation: Bhishma has heard everything — the needling of Drona, the doubt about his own protection — and answers none of it with words. He roars and blows his conch: a grandfather steadying a frightened grandchild the only way a warrior can. The gesture is pure affection and pure tragedy; the cheer he gives Duryodhana is the war's starting gun.
verses.connection: Bhishma responds to the anxiety of 1.10–11 not with argument but with sound.
verses.reflection: Sometimes the kindest act for an anxious person is one clear, confident sound — be that for someone.
verses.background: Duryodhana's speech ends, and Sanjaya turns to Bhishma, eldest of the Kuru line and commander of the Kaurava army. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as Bhishma's response on hearing the king's respectful words.
verses.hook: How does Bhishma respond to Duryodhana's anxiety?

views.text: Sees Bhishma's roar as a response to Duryodhana's despondency: noticing his gloom, the grandsire roars and has his side sound their instruments as a sign of victory, to cheer him.
Describes Duryodhana's speech as respectful (bahumāna-yuktam); Bhishma, hearing it, answers by raising the king's spirits with a great lion-roar and his conch.
Bhishma knows Duryodhana cannot win with Krishna on the other side, yet out of affection he blows his conch to cheer him and signal that he will fight faithfully.

verses.devanagari:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः ।
सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत्॥
verses.transliteration:
tataḥ śaṅkhāśca bheryaśca paṇavānakagomukhāḥ
sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śabdastumulo'bhavat
verses.essence: Then the whole Kaurava host erupts — conches, drums, horns — a sudden tumult.
verses.translation: Then (following Bhishma), conches and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow horns blared forth quite suddenly (from the Kaurava side) and the sound was tremendous.

anvaya.base: पणव · tabor; आनक · drum; गोमुख · cow-horn trumpet
anvaya.parts: पणव (tabor) + आनक (drum) + गोमुख (cow-horn): tabors, drums and cow-horns (a list compound)

verses.explanation: One conch becomes an avalanche. The whole Kaurava host answers its commander at once — conches, kettledrums, tabors, cow-horns — and the verse calls the result tumulaḥ, a tumult: enormous, sudden, without shape. Remember this noise. In the next verse the other side answers, and the text slows down to name each conch and the man who blows it.
verses.connection: Bhishma's single note from the previous verse is amplified into the roar of an army.
verses.reflection: Notice how quickly one bold note becomes a chorus; your tone sets more weather than you think.
verses.background: Bhishma's conch has just sounded. Śrīdhara presents this verse as the whole Kaurava army catching its commander's eagerness for battle, so that its instruments take up his signal at once.
verses.hook: What happens in the Kaurava army after Bhishma blows his conch?

views.text: Links the din to the commander: seeing Bhishma's eagerness for battle, a festive war-mood broke out on every side, and all the instruments were struck at that very moment.

verses.devanagari:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ ।
माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः॥
verses.transliteration:
tataḥ śvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau
mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaścaiva divyau śaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ
verses.essence: Then, from a great chariot yoked with white horses, Krishna and Arjuna answer.
verses.translation: Then, also, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in the magnificent chariot, yoked with white horses, blew divine conches.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative dual (the two, standing)
verb, perfect (past), 3rd person dual (the two blew)

verses.explanation: The camera turns, and everything sharpens. Against the anonymous tumult: one chariot, white horses, two figures, two conches — and the word divyau, divine. This is the Gita's first glimpse of Krishna, and he appears exactly as he will remain: not commanding the army, but standing beside Arjuna. The story's true centre enters without saying a word.
verses.connection: The Kaurava wall of sound meets its answer — smaller, clearer, and qualitatively other.
verses.reflection: Amid today's noise, listen for the one calm, clear voice that answers without shouting, and let it set your pace.
verses.background: The din of the Kaurava instruments is dying away, and Sanjaya turns to the Pandava side. Śrīdhara says the next five verses describe its own call to battle, beginning with the two who stand in one chariot: Krishna, driving it, and Arjuna.
verses.hook: How do Krishna and Arjuna answer the Kaurava uproar?

views.text: Stresses who is on that chariot: Krishna, Lord of all lords, serving as Arjuna's charioteer in a great chariot able to conquer the three worlds, answers the Kaurava uproar with his divine conch.
Places the verse as the start of the Pandava answer, after the Kaurava din; pra-dadhmatuḥ means the two blew their conches with full force.
Calling Krishna Madhava, the husband of Lakshmi, hints that the goddess of fortune is with the Pandavas and that they will win back their kingdom.

verses.devanagari:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनञ्जयः ।
पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः॥
verses.transliteration:
pāñcajanyaṃ hṛṣīkeśo devadattaṃ dhanañjayaḥ
pauṇḍraṃ dadhmau mahāśaṅkhaṃ bhīmakarmā vṛkodaraḥ
verses.essence: Krishna sounds Panchajanya, Arjuna Devadatta, Bhima his great conch Paundra.
verses.translation: Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya and Arjuna blew the Devadatta and Bhima (the wolf-bellied), the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.

anvaya.parts: हृषीक (senses) + ईश (lord): lord of the senses
धनम् (wealth) + जय (winning): winner of wealth
महा (great) + शङ्ख (conch): great conch
भीम (terrible) + कर्मन् (deed): one whose deeds are terrible
वृक (wolf) + उदर (belly): one with a belly like a wolf's

verses.explanation: On this side, every conch has a name and a story — Panchajanya taken from a slain demon, Devadatta given by the gods. A named instrument is an identity, not just noise. And the verse names Krishna 'Hrishikesha', master of the senses: the Gita's quiet signal of who is actually holding the reins of that chariot.
verses.connection: The two divine conches of the previous verse are now named — sound becoming signature.
verses.reflection: Before a hard conversation, find your conch — the breath or word that announces you are fully here.
verses.background: Sanjaya has said that Krishna and Arjuna blew divine conches; now he names each conch with its player, and adds Bhima, called Vrikodara, 'wolf-bellied', as the next to sound.
verses.hook: Which conches do Krishna, Arjuna and Bhima sound?

views.text: Notes that Panchajanya and the rest are the proper names of the conches, and explains Bhima's epithets: bhīmakarmā, whose deeds are terrible, and vṛkodara, whose belly is like a wolf's.
The name Hrishikesha marks Krishna as the master of everyone's mind and senses, a mastery he showed throughout his life.

verses.devanagari:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः ।
नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ॥
verses.transliteration:
anantavijayaṃ rājā kuntīputro yudhiṣṭhiraḥ
nakulaḥ sahadevaśca sughoṣamaṇipuṣpakau
verses.essence: Yudhishthira sounds Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva, Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
verses.translation: The king Yodhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.

anvaya.parts: अनन्त (endless) + विजय (victory): endless victory
कुन्ती (Kunti) + पुत्र (son): Kunti's son

anvaya.base: सुघोष, मणिपुष्पक · names of the twins' conches
anvaya.parts: सुघोष (sweet-sounding) + मणिपुष्पक (jewel-flowered): the two conches, a pair compound

verses.explanation: Even here the text is precise about character: Yudhishthira — the king who never wanted this war — sounds a conch named 'endless victory', as if the name must carry the conviction he lacks. The twins follow with theirs. Five brothers, five distinct voices: the Pandava answer is a chord, not a roar.
verses.connection: The naming continues down the line of brothers.
verses.reflection: Notice where you lean on a bold title or slogan to carry a conviction you do not quite feel.
verses.background: The naming of Pandava conches moves past Krishna, Arjuna and Bhima to the remaining brothers: Yudhishthira, the eldest, whom Sanjaya calls king, and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva.
verses.hook: Which conches do Yudhishthira and the twins blow?

views.text: Assigns the conches in order: Nakula blew the one named Sughosha, Sahadeva the one named Manipushpaka.
Sanjaya calls Yudhishthira 'king' for his royal bearing, and calls Dhritarashtra lord of the earth to remind him that he alone could still stop this war.

verses.devanagari:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः ।
धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः॥
verses.transliteration:
kāśyaśca parameṣvāsaḥ śikhaṇḍī ca mahārathaḥ
dhṛṣṭadyumno virāṭaśca sātyakiścāparājitaḥ
verses.essence: The king of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, unconquered Satyaki —
verses.translation: The king of Kasi, an excellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna and Virata and Satyaki, the unconquered.

anvaya.parts: परम (supreme) + इष्वास (bow): one whose bow is supreme
महा (great) + रथ (chariot): a top-rank warrior

anvaya.base: विराट · Virata, king of the Matsyas

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: Among the names, one is a slow fuse: Shikhandi — born to destroy Bhishma, the one fighter the grandsire has vowed never to strike. The same Bhishma whose conch opened the war, and around whom Duryodhana built his whole defence, has his appointed end standing in this verse, sounding a conch of his own.
verses.connection: The brothers' conches give way to their allies'; among them is Shikhandi, the warrior behind whom Bhishma, who began the noise in 1.12, will fall.
verses.reflection: Even supporting roles get named in this roll-call. Whose quiet contribution can you name aloud today?
verses.background: With the five brothers' conches named, Sanjaya turns to the allied commanders of the Pandava army. This verse carries the first of them, among them Shikhandi and the marshal Dhrishtadyumna; the sentence runs on into the next verse.
verses.hook: Which other Pandava allies join in sounding their conches?

views.text: Glosses kāśya as the king of Kashi and parameṣvāsa as one whose bow is the finest, reading the line as the continuing roll of Pandava conch-blowers.
By addressing Dhritarashtra as ruler of the earth, Sanjaya quietly reminds him that the coming destruction is still his to prevent.

verses.devanagari:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते ।
सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक्॥
verses.transliteration:
drupado draupadeyāśca sarvaśaḥ pṛthivīpate
saubhadraśca mahābāhuḥ śaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛthakpṛthak
verses.essence: — Drupada, Draupadi's sons, Abhimanyu: each blows his own conch, one by one.
verses.translation: Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the earth, and the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches separately.

anvaya.base: द्रुपद · Drupada, king of the Panchalas
पृथिवीपति · lord of the earth, king
anvaya.parts: पृथिवी (earth) + पति (lord): lord of the earth
महा (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty

verses.explanation: Pṛthak pṛthak — 'each one, separately'. The phrase ends the conch passage and quietly states its meaning: on this side every person sounds as himself, distinct, accountable. Sanjaya slips in 'O lord of the earth', reminding us a blind king is hearing all this — hearing his enemies, one by one, refuse to be a faceless mass.
verses.connection: The roll of conches completes — a chord of individuals against the earlier tumult.
verses.reflection: A cause becomes real when each helper sounds separately — invite one silent supporter to speak.
verses.background: The list of allies sounding their conches ends with Drupada, the five sons of Draupadi and Abhimanyu. In the middle of it Sanjaya addresses the blind king directly, as 'lord of the earth'.
verses.hook: Do all the Pandava warriors join in sounding their conches?

views.text: Notes only that 'lord of the earth' addresses Dhritarashtra: Sanjaya is speaking to the blind king throughout.
Takes this round of conches as the formal announcement that the battle has begun.
As every Pandava ally sounds his conch, Sanjaya's words press the blind king to see that only he can still halt the war.

verses.devanagari:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत् ।
नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलो व्यनुनादयन्॥
verses.transliteration:
sa ghoṣo dhārtarāṣṭrāṇāṃ hṛdayāni vyadārayat
nabhaśca pṛthivīṃ caiva tumulo vyanunādayan
verses.essence: That sound tears through the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons, shaking sky and earth.
verses.translation: That tumultuous sound rent the hearts of (the members of) Dhritarashtra's party, making both the heaven and the earth resound.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while making resound)

verses.explanation: The larger army made noise; the smaller one made meaning — and meaning is what tears hearts. Sanjaya says it to Dhritarashtra's face: your sons' hearts split before a single arrow flew. Battles are decided in the chest first. The Kauravas' sound filled the air; the Pandavas' sound entered people.
verses.connection: The answer to the tumult of 1.13 lands — and the verse measures the difference in hearts, not decibels.
verses.reflection: Some sounds rend hearts that armor cannot reach. Choose your words today knowing this.
verses.background: Every Pandava conch has now sounded. Sanjaya reports to Dhritarashtra what that sound did, and Śrīdhara notes that he speaks of the Kaurava side to the king as 'yours'.
verses.text_note: Some editions read tumulo ’bhyanunādayan; Gita Supersite and the critical edition read tumulo vyanunādayan (used here).
verses.hook: What effect does the Pandava conch-blast have on Dhritarashtra's sons?

views.text: Draws out what Sanjaya implies: the tumult rent the hearts of Duryodhana and his brothers, who thought their cause already almost lost, said to a king who longed for their victory.
Stresses that the sound bred great fear in 'your people' (tvadīyānām), Sanjaya pointedly addressing Dhritarashtra about his own sons.
The Pandava conches shatter the Kauravas' hearts because a guilty conscience weakens them, while the Pandavas feel secure with Krishna on their side.

verses.devanagari:
अथ व्यवस्थितान्दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान् कपिध्वजः ।
प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसम्पाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः॥
verses.transliteration:
atha vyavasthitāndṛṣṭvā dhārtarāṣṭrān kapidhvajaḥ
pravṛtte śastrasampāte dhanurudyamya pāṇḍavaḥ
verses.essence: As weapons are about to fly, Arjuna, the monkey-bannered, sees the Kauravas arrayed and lifts his bow.
verses.translation: Then, seeing the people of Dhritarashtra’s party standing arrayed and the discharge of weapons about to begin, Arjuna, the son of Pandu, whose ensign was a monkey, took up his bow and said the following to Krishna, O Lord of the earth.

anvaya.base: वि-अव-√स्था · to be drawn up, stationed
कपिध्वज · one with a monkey on his flag
anvaya.parts: कपि (monkey, Hanuman) + ध्वज (banner): one whose banner bears the monkey

anvaya.base: प्र-√वृत् · to begin, set in motion
anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, locative singular (when ..., with the next word)

anvaya.parts: शस्त्र (weapon) + सम्पात (flying together, discharge): the flight of weapons

verses.explanation: The moment is a knife's edge: weapons are launching, the bow is already raised — and instead of an arrow, words come out. Everything that follows, all seven hundred verses, happens inside this raised-bow instant. The epic slows time at its most violent point to make room for a conversation.
verses.connection: Out of the fading conch-roar, the story narrows to one man, one bow, one turning toward Krishna.
verses.reflection: At the very edge of action, lift your eyes once more and look — really look — at what you face.
verses.background: The conches have fallen silent, the armies stand in order and weapons are about to fly. Sanjaya turns to Arjuna, whose banner bears a monkey; Śrīdhara takes this verse and the next three as Arjuna's request to Krishna at that moment.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna do as the weapons are about to clash?

views.text: Dwells on the banner: Arjuna's flag bears Hanuman, famed for burning Lanka, a reminder of the strength standing behind the Pandava chariot.
Introduces verses 1.20-1.23 as Arjuna respectfully informing Krishna (vijñāpayāmāsa) of his wish, not simply issuing an order; vyavasthitān means drawn up ready for battle.
Arjuna's flag bears Hanuman, who humbled him over his pride in archery and promised to ride on his chariot in the great war.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत॥
verses.transliteration:
hṛṣīkeśaṃ tadā vākyamidamāha mahīpate
senayorubhayormadhye rathaṃ sthāpaya me'cyuta
verses.essence: Arjuna's first words: place my chariot between the two armies, Achyuta.
verses.translation: In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot, O krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, accusative singular (to whom he spoke)
anvaya.parts: हृषीक (senses) + ईश (lord): lord of the senses

anvaya.base: महीपति · lord of the earth, king
anvaya.parts: मही (earth) + पति (lord): lord of the earth

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, genitive dual (of the two)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + च्युत (fallen): one who never falls

verses.explanation: The first spoken sentence of the Gita's hero is an order to God — and Krishna will simply obey it. Arjuna asks to be taken to the exact centre, the place of maximum exposure where neither side can claim him. He calls Krishna 'Achyuta', the one who never falls: he is about to fall, and some part of him is already reaching for the one who can't.
verses.connection: The words promised in the previous verse arrive — not a war cry, but a request to see.
verses.reflection: Ask to be taken to the middle of your conflict, not briefed from its safe edge.
verses.background: With the armies poised, Arjuna, bow lifted, speaks for the first time in the poem. He addresses Krishna, who is serving as his charioteer, with an instruction about where the chariot should go.
verses.text_note: The half-verse hṛṣīkeśaṃ tadā vākyam… is counted with 1.20 in some editions; placed in 1.21 here, as in Gita Supersite and the critical edition. Sivananda translates 1.21 and 1.22 as one sentence, so the same translation appears on both verses.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna first ask Krishna to do on the battlefield?

refs.note: God says that though fully independent, he becomes bound by his devotees' love; this is why Krishna accepts Arjuna's orders as his charioteer.

views.text: Marvels that the one taking this instruction is the Supreme Lord, source of the cosmos and controller of every sense, who out of love for those who take refuge in him serves as Arjuna's charioteer.
That the Lord himself drives Arjuna's chariot and takes his orders shows how God, though independent, lets himself be bound by a devotee's love.

verses.devanagari:
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान् ।
कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन् रणसमुद्यमे॥
verses.transliteration:
yāvadetānnirīkṣe'haṃ yoddhukāmānavasthitān
kairmayā saha yoddhavyamasmin raṇasamudyame
verses.essence: Let me look at the men I am to fight, who stand here desiring battle.
verses.translation: In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot, O krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.

anvaya.form: verb, present, 1st person singular, middle voice

anvaya.parts: योद्धुम् (to fight) + काम (desire): those who want to fight

anvaya.form: pronoun, interrogative, masculine instrumental plural (with whom)
gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (it must be done)

anvaya.parts: रण (battle) + समुद्यम (undertaking): the undertaking of battle

verses.explanation: Nirīkṣe — not 'see' but 'inspect closely'. Arjuna thinks he is doing reconnaissance: assessing opponents the way a professional assesses targets. But he frames it as 'with whom must I fight' — yoddhavyam, a duty, something imposed. The soldier's question is already carrying a philosopher's weight, and he doesn't know it yet.
verses.connection: He explains the request of 1.21 — wanting to convert enemies from a mass into knowable men.
verses.reflection: Before opposing anyone, grant yourself one unhurried look at exactly whom you oppose.
verses.background: Arjuna's request to Krishna continues into its purpose. Śrīdhara frames it against an implied objection: a warrior's task is to fight, not to watch, so why drive out to look at the armies?
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna want his chariot placed between the armies?

refs.note: God says that though fully independent, he becomes bound by his devotees' love; this is why Krishna accepts Arjuna's orders as his charioteer.

views.text: Raises the objection 'you are a fighter, not a spectator of the battle' and answers it from the verse: Arjuna wants to see precisely with whom he must fight.
Arjuna directs Krishna like a servant here, a picture of how the Lord becomes subservient to those who love him.

verses.text_note: Sivananda translates 1.21 and 1.22 as one sentence, so the same translation appears on both verses.

verses.devanagari:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः॥
verses.transliteration:
yotsyamānānavekṣe'haṃ ya ete'tra samāgatāḥ
dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheryuddhe priyacikīrṣavaḥ
verses.essence: I want to see who has gathered here to please Duryodhana's wicked mind by fighting.
verses.translation: For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana (the son of Dhritarashtra).

anvaya.form: future participle, masculine, accusative plural (who will fight)
verb, present, 1st person singular, middle voice

anvaya.parts: दुर् (bad) + बुद्धि (mind): one whose mind is wicked

anvaya.base: प्रियचिकीर्षु · wishing to do what is dear
anvaya.parts: प्रिय (what is dear) + चिकीर्षु (wishing to do, from √कृ): wanting to do what pleases him

verses.explanation: Listen to the armour in his voice: the enemy are toadies of 'evil-minded Duryodhana'. Contempt is how a warrior keeps the enemy abstract — they chose the villain, so they can be killed. This is the last verse in which Arjuna manages to see the other side as a category. The armour is about to meet their faces.
verses.connection: He sharpens the inspection of 1.22 with moral contempt — the mind bracing itself to kill.
verses.reflection: Notice who shows up to please the powerful rather than from conviction — beginning with yourself.
verses.background: The last verse of Arjuna's request, spoken before the chariot moves. Having asked to see his opponents, he describes them as the men who have come to Kurukshetra to serve Duryodhana's cause.
verses.hook: Whom does Arjuna want to look at before the fighting starts?

views.text: Construes 1.21-1.23 as one sentence: 'place my chariot between the armies until I have seen those gathered here to please Duryodhana', naming the evil-minded son as Duryodhana.
Still fearless, Arjuna wants a close look at everyone who has sided with injustice, meaning to punish them all for backing Duryodhana.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम्॥
verses.transliteration:
evamukto hṛṣīkeśo guḍākeśena bhārata
senayorubhayormadhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam
verses.essence: So spoken to, Krishna drives the great chariot between the two armies.
verses.translation: Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna, having stationed that best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (having been told)

anvaya.parts: हृषीक (senses) + ईश (lord): lord of the senses
गुडाका (sleep) + ईश (master): master of sleep

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, genitive dual (of the two)

anvaya.parts: रथ (chariot) + उत्तम (best): the best of chariots

verses.explanation: Sanjaya chooses the names with a poet's irony: Gudakesha, the man who has conquered sleep, gives an order; Hrishikesha, the master of the senses, carries it out. The Lord of everything works as a driver — and by obeying, he steers Arjuna to the one spot on earth where his certainty cannot survive. Sometimes grace looks exactly like doing what you're told.
verses.connection: Krishna answers the request of 1.21 — with an obedience that is really a teaching.
verses.reflection: When someone asks to see things plainly, honor it as Krishna did: drive them to the center.
verses.background: Sanjaya takes up the narrative again, telling Dhritarashtra what happened next. Krishna has heard Arjuna, whom Sanjaya calls Gudakesha, 'conqueror of sleep', and now acts on his request.
verses.hook: What does Krishna do once Arjuna asks him to move the chariot?

views.text: Notes that Krishna did at once exactly as Arjuna directed, in full view of Bhishma, Drona and the kings, adding Sanjaya's irony to the blind king: such is the prospect of victory for your men.
Explains guḍākeśa as guḍākā (sleep) plus īśa (master): Arjuna, who has conquered sleep; bhārata addresses Dhritarashtra.

verses.devanagari:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम् ।
उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति॥
verses.transliteration:
bhīṣmadroṇapramukhataḥ sarveṣāṃ ca mahīkṣitām
uvāca pārtha paśyaitānsamavetānkurūniti
verses.essence: Facing Bhishma and Drona, Krishna says: behold, Partha, these Kurus gathered here.
verses.translation: In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, said: "O Arjuna (son of Pritha), behold these Kurus gathered together."

anvaya.meaning: in front of Bhishma and Drona
anvaya.parts: भीष्म (Bhishma) + द्रोण (Drona) + प्रमुख (front) + -तः (at): in front of Bhishma and Drona

anvaya.meaning: of the rulers of the earth
anvaya.base: महीक्षित् · ruler of the earth, king
anvaya.parts: मही (earth) + क्षित् (ruling): rulers of the earth

anvaya.base: thus (marks the end of quoted words)

verses.explanation: Krishna could have stopped the chariot anywhere along the line. He stops it precisely before Bhishma and Drona — the grandfather who raised Arjuna and the teacher who made him an archer — and says only one short line: behold these assembled Kurus. Not 'the enemy', not 'the Kauravas'. Kurus — the family name Arjuna himself shares. The word is a scalpel. Krishna is not causing Arjuna's crisis; he is refusing to let him postpone it.
verses.connection: Arjuna asked to see whom he must fight (1.21–22); Krishna sets him before Bhishma and Drona and calls them all 'Kurus', Arjuna's own family name.
verses.reflection: Life sometimes parks you directly facing your teachers and elders as obstacles. Stay parked a moment.
verses.background: The chariot comes to rest between the armies. Sanjaya tells the king exactly where Krishna has placed it, directly in front of Bhishma, Drona and the other kings of the Kaurava side, and reports Krishna's first words on the field.
verses.hook: What does Krishna tell Arjuna to look at between the armies?

views.text: Spells out where the chariot stopped: directly in front of the grandsire, Drona and the kings, and only then did Krishna say 'Partha, see these Kurus'.
By calling the enemy 'Kurus', Krishna deliberately reminds Arjuna that they are his own family, sowing a confusion he will later remove through the Gita's teaching.

verses.devanagari:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितॄनथ पितामहान् ।
आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातॄन्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा॥
verses.transliteration:
tatrāpaśyatsthitānpārthaḥ pitṝnatha pitāmahān
ācāryānmātulānbhrātṝnputrānpautrānsakhīṃstathā
verses.essence: There Arjuna sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends.
verses.translation: Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends too.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, accusative plural (describes the people seen)

verses.explanation: The verse is almost nothing but a list, and that is its power. Arjuna looked for 'the ones who wish to fight' (1.22) — an army, a category. What he finds is relationships: fathers, grandfathers, uncles, brothers, sons, and the teachers and friends who are family in all but blood. The abstraction 'enemy' dissolves into faces he has known his whole life. War is possible against categories; it becomes almost impossible against names.
verses.connection: He asked to inspect an army (1.23); what he actually sees is his family arranged for slaughter.
verses.reflection: In today's opposition, find the relative: the familiar face inside the unfamiliar position.
verses.background: Krishna has told Arjuna to look at the gathered Kurus. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as what followed, and Sanjaya lists the people Arjuna sees in the ranks, including the sons and grandsons of Duryodhana and his brothers.
verses.hook: Whom does Arjuna actually see standing in both armies?

views.text: Takes 'fathers' to mean paternal uncles and the like, and the sons and grandsons as those of Duryodhana and his brothers: Arjuna recognises his own family in the opposing ranks.

verses.devanagari:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि ।
तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान्॥
verses.transliteration:
śvaśurānsuhṛdaścaiva senayorubhayorapi
tānsamīkṣya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvānbandhūnavasthitān
verses.essence: Fathers-in-law, well-wishers, in both armies — seeing all these kinsmen arrayed, Arjuna is overcome.
verses.translation: (He saw) fathers-in-law and friends also in both the armies. The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed, spoke this, sorrowfully filled with deep pity.

anvaya.parts: सु (good) + हृद् (heart): one whose heart is kind

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, locative dual (in the two)
past participle, masculine, accusative plural (describes बन्धून्)

verses.explanation: Two small words finish the catastrophe: ubhayoḥ api — in both armies. Until now a side could still be chosen; kin here, foes there. The seeing (samīkṣya — looking thoroughly, not glancing) erases the line down the middle of the field. Whoever wins, Arjuna's family loses. The military map and the map of love no longer match, and he is standing on both at once.
verses.connection: The list of 1.26 spills over the battle-line itself: the kinship terms continue, but now on both sides.
verses.reflection: When you see that people on both sides of a conflict are yours, notice what shifts in you, and name it before acting.
verses.background: Sanjaya finishes the list of those Arjuna sees in both armies and turns to Arjuna himself. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as the answer to 'then what did he do?', as grief takes hold of him.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna react on seeing his relatives arrayed for battle?

views.text: Glosses suhṛdaḥ as those who had once done Arjuna a kindness, benefactors rather than mere friends, which deepens the cost of facing them.
Krishna's word has its effect: the warrior eager to punish the Kauravas now sees only relatives, his courage fades, and Sanjaya calls him son of Kunti to mark his softened heart.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
कृपया परयाविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत् ।
दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdannidamabravīt
dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṃ samupasthitam
verses.essence: Filled with deepest pity, despairing, Arjuna speaks: seeing my own people ready to fight, Krishna —
verses.translation: Seeing these, my kinsmen, O krishna, arrayed, eager to fight.

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (describes Arjuna)
present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while sinking)
noun, masculine, accusative singular (object; a collective)
anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + जन (people): one's own people

anvaya.base: √युध् · to fight (desire form: wanting to fight)
सम्-उप-√स्था · to come together, be present
anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, accusative singular (describes स्वजनम्)

verses.explanation: The word for what floods Arjuna is kṛpā — pity, tenderness — and the grammar says it takes hold of him: āviṣṭaḥ, entered, pervaded, possessed. This is not a decision he makes; it is a state that seizes him. Notice too what wounds him most: svajanam yuyutsum — my own people, *wanting* to fight. Not just that they will die, but that they are eager for it. And in its very first line the lament calls out to Krishna, the friend who will answer it. The chapter's closing title, Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga, counts even this despair as a yoga: only a self honestly broken open can receive.
verses.connection: The seeing of 1.26–27 now becomes speech: Arjuna talks until 1.46, and Sanjaya takes the narration back only at the chapter's close in 1.47.
verses.reflection: Notice when a feeling seizes you rather than being chosen; name it as it arrives, before it starts speaking for you.
verses.background: Overcome by what he has just seen, Arjuna turns to Krishna on the chariot and begins a lament that will fill the rest of the chapter. His first words still look out at the ranks in front of him.
verses.hook: What feeling overcomes Arjuna as he begins to speak to Krishna?

views.text: Sees Arjuna's collapse as coming from his nobility: kind, friendly and righteous, he is overcome by love and compassion for his relatives, and by fear of not knowing what is right and what is wrong.
Glosses āviṣṭaḥ as 'pervaded' by pity, and viṣīdan as sinking right down into exhaustion and dejection, a sinking rather than a single blow.
Arjuna's grief springs from attachment to bodily relatives; forgetting he is the soul, he loses sight of God as his only lasting relative.

verses.devanagari:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति ।
वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते॥
verses.transliteration:
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṃ ca pariśuṣyati
vepathuśca śarīre me romaharṣaśca jāyate
verses.essence: My limbs give way, my mouth dries up, my body trembles, my hair stands on end.
verses.translation: My limbs fail and my mouth is parched, my body quivers and my hair stands on end.

anvaya.base: परि-√शुष् · to dry up all over

anvaya.parts: रोमन् (body hair) + हर्ष (bristling): the hair standing on end

verses.explanation: Before Arjuna offers a single argument, his body argues for him. The Gita is precise about the physiology of anguish: failing limbs, dry mouth, tremor, bristling hair — a clinical description of what we would call an acute stress response. The text honors something we often forget: a worldview crisis is not first an intellectual event. It happens in the flesh, and the mind's reasons come limping after.
verses.connection: From 'my own people' (1.28) the camera turns inward: what that sight does to a body.
verses.reflection: Dry mouth, racing heart — greet the body's panic by name today instead of pretending composure.
verses.background: Arjuna has just told Krishna that he sees his kinsmen ready to fight. Still standing in the chariot between the armies, he goes on to describe what is happening to him as he speaks.
verses.hook: What happens to Arjuna's body when he faces his kinsmen?

views.text: Glosses the symptoms plainly: hands and feet give way and fall slack, the mouth loses all moisture, vepathu is shaking and romaharṣa the thrill of hair standing up.
The thought of killing his relatives disturbs Arjuna so deeply that even this famed warrior begins to tremble.

verses.devanagari:
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते ।
न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः॥
verses.transliteration:
gāṇḍīvaṃ sraṃsate hastāttvakcaiva paridahyate
na ca śaknomyavasthātuṃ bhramatīva ca me manaḥ
verses.essence: Gandiva slips from my hand, my skin burns, I cannot stand, my mind reels.
verses.translation: The (bow) Gandiva slips from my hand, and also my skins burns all over; I am unable even to stand and my mind is reeling, as it were.

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is burned)

verses.explanation: Gandiva was Arjuna's identity made of wood and string — the bow that made him the world's archer. When it slips from his hand, the warrior-self slips with it. The sequence in these two verses runs body → bow → mind: first the flesh fails, then the instrument of his role, finally thought itself (bhramati — wanders, spins). The crisis is not of strength but of meaning: the bow falls unfought, because no muscle can grip what the heart has dropped.
verses.connection: Completes the symptom-list of 1.29 and ends at the mind — preparing the mental 'omens' of the next verse.
verses.reflection: Notice the order in which stress takes you today: body first, then your grip on tasks, then clear thinking.
verses.background: Arjuna's account of his own collapse continues, addressed to Krishna. The great bow Gandiva, lifted when he asked for the chariot to move out, is still in his hands as his strength and composure give way.
verses.hook: Why can Arjuna no longer hold his bow or stand steady?

views.text: Glosses sraṃsate as 'falls down' and paridahyate as 'is scorched on every side': the bow drops and the burning is felt over the whole body.
Arjuna's distress is so great he cannot grip his mighty bow, and his shaken mind starts reading bad omens everywhere.

verses.devanagari:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव ।
न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे॥
verses.transliteration:
nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni keśava
na ca śreyo'nupaśyāmi hatvā svajanamāhave
verses.essence: I see omens of evil, Keshava; I see no good in killing my own people in battle.
verses.translation: And I see adverse omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good in killing my kinsmen in battle.

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + जन (people): one's own people

verses.explanation: A whirling mind starts reading the world as a text of doom: nimittāni, omens. But buried in Arjuna's panic is the Gita's most important word making its first appearance — śreyas, the truly good, the highest welfare, as opposed to mere pleasure or gain. Arjuna is right that he cannot see śreyas in this slaughter. His error, the chapters ahead will show, is in where he is looking for it. The question 'what is śreyas?' is the engine of the entire dialogue.
verses.connection: The reeling mind of 1.30 projects outward as omens, and lands on the word 'good' that returns in 2.7, when Arjuna asks Krishna what is good for him.
verses.reflection: Notice the omens you collect when you already want to quit — fear is a skilled curator.
verses.background: Shaken in body and mind, Arjuna still speaks to Krishna, here calling him Keshava. From his own condition he turns, for the first time, to weighing what the coming battle could bring.
verses.hook: What good does Arjuna expect from killing his own people?

views.text: Hears a hidden premise in the objection: killing people seen as 'my teachers, my kin' must breed sin. Krishna's reply will be to act simply as one's own duty, without that individualizing idea.
Glosses śreyas here simply as phala, a fruit or result: Arjuna sees no gain at all coming from killing his own people in battle.
Overcome by delusion, Arjuna sees only ill omens and concludes that fighting this battle would be a sin.

verses.devanagari:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च ।
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा॥
verses.transliteration:
na kāṅkṣe vijayaṃ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṃ sukhāni ca
kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā
verses.essence: I desire no victory, Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. What is kingdom to us, what enjoyment, or life itself?
verses.translation: I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what avail is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life?

anvaya.form: pronoun, question word, neuter singular (what use?)
pronoun, question word, neuter singular (what use?)

verses.explanation: Arjuna begins to reason, and his reasoning is not foolish — it is the logic of means and ends. Victory, kingdom, pleasure are means; people are the ends for whom one wants them. The rhetorical questions (kim... kim...) escalate from kingdom to enjoyment to life itself: a man auditing his motivations and finding every account empty. This is genuine insight into the hollowness of prizes — arrived at, however, in a way that conveniently argues for walking away.
verses.connection: Having seen no good in fighting (1.31), he now dismantles the ordinary reasons for it: victory, kingdom and pleasure.
verses.reflection: Ask honestly: is there a victory you are chasing whose taste you no longer want?
verses.background: Arjuna has said he sees no good in killing his kin. Śrīdhara sets this verse against the question 'do you not see its fruits, victory and the rest?', and Arjuna answers by turning to the very prizes the war is meant to win.
verses.hook: Does Arjuna still want victory, a kingdom or pleasure?

views.text: Notes the second strand of Arjuna's worry: even justified killing, if fought for apparent results like pleasure and kingdom, generates sin. Krishna will answer by asking for action done as duty, not for its results.
Frames the verse as Arjuna's answer to an implied question, 'do you not see the fruits, victory and the rest?': he replies that he does not even want them.
Arjuna's indifference to victory sounds virtuous, but it comes from attachment to his kin, not spiritual insight, which would bring peace rather than confusion.

verses.devanagari:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च ।
त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च॥
verses.transliteration:
yeṣāmarthe kāṅkṣitaṃ no rājyaṃ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca
ta ime'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca
verses.essence: Those for whose sake we want kingdom and pleasures stand here in battle, staking life and wealth.
verses.translation: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures, stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, masculine, genitive plural (of whom)
noun, masculine, locative singular (for the sake of)
past participle, neuter, nominative singular (is desired)
pronoun, plural, short form (here: by us)
past participle, masculine, nominative plural (are standing)

verses.explanation: Here the means-end logic closes its circle. A kingdom is wanted *for* one's people — teachers, fathers, sons. But the very people who give the prize its meaning are the ones who must be killed to win it. Victory would hand Arjuna a feast with no one left to share it. As a piece of reasoning it is airtight; what it quietly assumes is that family happiness is the highest end there is. That assumption is what Krishna will eventually question.
verses.connection: Answers the rhetorical 'what use is kingdom?' of 1.32: its purpose stands on the field, about to die.
verses.reflection: List what you are sacrificing your peace for — then ask who that prize was originally for.
verses.background: Still facing the ranks, Arjuna keeps arguing with Krishna about the prizes of war. Here he ties those prizes to the people now standing across the field from him.
verses.hook: Who are the people for whose sake a kingdom is worth having?

views.text: Reads 1.32–34 as one thought: the very people for whom kingdom and pleasure are wanted have resolved to give up life and wealth in battle, so what would a kingdom do for us?
Arjuna's reasoning is moral but not spiritual: a victory that costs everyone who matters to him seems joyless, and his mind is losing its balance.

verses.devanagari:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः ।
मातुलाः श्वशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा॥
verses.transliteration:
ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāstathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ
mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ sambandhinastathā
verses.essence: Teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers, uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, kinsmen —
verses.translation: Teachers, fathers, sons and also grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other relatives,-
verses.explanation: Arjuna repeats, nearly item for item, the list Sanjaya gave in 1.26 — but now in his own mouth, and with brothers-in-law and other kin added. What the narrator described, the sufferer now recites, like a man counting his wounds aloud. The list returning means the sight has lodged in him and become his inner inventory. Grief always keeps lists.
verses.connection: Sanjaya's catalogue of 1.26 returns in first person — observation has become lament.
verses.reflection: The people entangled in your hardest decision: say their names slowly, and let the weight be real.
verses.background: Arjuna has said that those for whose sake a kingdom is wanted stand ready to die. He now names them, in a list of relations that runs on into the next verse, where his refusal comes.
verses.hook: Which relatives and elders does Arjuna see ready to die in battle?

views.text: Arjuna surveys his teachers, great-uncles, uncles, cousins and their families, all gathered for a fight to the death.

verses.devanagari:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन ।
अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते॥
verses.transliteration:
etānna hantumicchāmi ghnato'pi madhusūdana
api trailokyarājyasya hetoḥ kiṃ nu mahīkṛte
verses.essence: These I would not kill even if they kill me — not for the three worlds' kingdom, let alone the earth.
verses.translation: These I do not wish to kill, though they kill me, O Krishna, even for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing them for the sake of the earth.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, accusative plural (describes एतान्: while killing)

anvaya.parts: मधु (the demon Madhu) + सूदन (slayer): slayer of Madhu

verses.explanation: The argument peaks in a vow with real moral grandeur: better to be killed than to kill these. The escalation — not for the three worlds, so certainly not for this scrap of earth — shows Arjuna at his noblest. And the chosen name cuts both ways: he calls Krishna Madhusudana, slayer of the demon Madhu, even while renouncing slaying. As if to say: killing demons is your work; these are not demons, they are my grandfather.
verses.connection: The means-end argument of 1.32–34 reaches its absolute: no prize at any scale justifies this price.
verses.reflection: Name the people you would not harm for any prize, even a huge one, and let that set the size of your ambitions.
verses.background: The list of kin from 1.34 reaches its main verb. Śrīdhara sets the verse against an objection: if pity holds you back, they will kill you anyway out of greed for the kingdom, so kill them and rule. Arjuna answers it to Krishna.
verses.hook: Would Arjuna kill his kinsmen even to rule all three worlds?

views.text: Supplies the objection Arjuna answers: if pity stops you, they will kill you anyway out of greed, so kill them first and rule. Even so, he says, not for three worlds, much less mere earth.
Arjuna insists that even if they try to kill him, and even for all three worlds, killing his own people could bring him no joy.

verses.devanagari:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन ।
पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः॥
verses.transliteration:
nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrānnaḥ kā prītiḥ syājjanārdana
pāpamevāśrayedasmānhatvaitānātatāyinaḥ
verses.essence: What joy could come from slaying Dhritarashtra's sons? Sin alone would cling to us for killing these aggressors.
verses.translation: By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure can be ours, O Janardana? Only sin will accrue to us from killing these felons.

anvaya.form: pronoun, question word, feminine, nominative singular (what?)

verses.explanation: Arjuna now argues against the strongest case for war, and he knows the law he is bending. An ātatāyin — arsonist, poisoner, armed attacker, robber of wealth, land or wife — may lawfully be killed on sight, and Duryodhana's party has been all of these. Arjuna concedes the category ('these ātatāyins') and overrides it: lawful or not, the killing would stain us. He is setting one law against another — the rule that permits killing aggressors against the deeper dharma that forbids killing one's own elders and kin. It is his most sophisticated move, and still Krishna will not let it stand unexamined.
verses.connection: Extends the vow of 1.35 to even the legally killable: not just love, now dharma itself seems to forbid the war.
verses.reflection: Revenge promises relief and delivers residue. Recall once when winning left a film on everything.
verses.background: Arjuna meets a harder objection, from law. Śrīdhara spells it out: under the old rule naming six kinds of aggressor, among them arsonists, poisoners and those who seize land or wife, the Kauravas qualify, and killing an aggressor carries no blame.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna think he would gain by killing Dhritarashtra's sons?

Lists six kinds of aggressors, such as arsonists, poisoners and those seizing one's kingdom, whom it is permissible to kill.
Says killing an attacker in self-defence is not a sin, which qualifies Arjuna's argument against fighting the aggressors.

views.text: Reads 'sin would cling' as sin being the real agent: these enemies are already seized by sin, and killing them passes it to us. Sin here is greed's disregard for the ruin of the family.

Concedes they are ātatāyins under the six-fold definition, but holds that the rule allowing their killing is arthaśāstra, which Yājñavalkya ranks below dharmaśāstra; killing these elders and kin remains unjust and sinful.
Lists the ātatāyin as one who burns another's house, gives poison, rushes in with a sword, plunders wealth and land, or seizes another's wife, and notes that Duryodhana had done all of these.
Arjuna feels killing even these aggressors would be sin, yet scripture allows killing attackers in self-defence, so his scruple is not the whole truth.

verses.essence: Therefore we should not kill our own kinsmen. How could we be happy, Madhava, having slain our own people?
verses.translation: Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own people, O Madhava (Krishna)?

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + बान्धव (kinsman): our own relatives
स्व (own) + जन (people): one's own people

verses.explanation: Tasmāt — 'therefore' — the word of a man resting his case. But look at the verdict's final ground: sukhinaḥ syāma, 'could we be *happy*?' The argument that began with śreyas (the highest good, 1.31) quietly lands on sukha (happiness, comfort). The slippage is the tell. Arjuna's reasoning is sincere and humane, yet it cannot tell the difference between what is right and what he can bear. Teaching him that difference is the work Krishna takes up in chapter 2.
verses.connection: The 'therefore' gathers 1.31–36 into a verdict — whose ground has shifted from the good to the bearable.
verses.reflection: When you settle a hard question, check your final reason: is it what is right, or what will let you feel comfortable?
verses.background: Arjuna has just answered the legal case for killing the Kauravas. Calling Krishna Madhava, he now speaks of them simply as his own kin and sums up where his reasoning has brought him.
verses.hook: Why does Arjuna say he and his brothers should not kill their cousins?

refs.note: The Vedic injunction not to harm any living being, which underlies Arjuna's sense that killing his kin would be sinful.
Lists six kinds of aggressors, such as arsonists, poisoners and those seizing one's kingdom, whom it is permissible to kill.
Says killing an attacker in self-defence is not a sin, which qualifies Arjuna's argument against fighting the aggressors.

views.text: Locates the sin in the attitude: slaying done with a particularizing idea of the victim, 'these are my own kin', and with an eye on the result, is what makes it a great sin.
Arjuna's refusal rests on kinship: he cannot see how killing his own people could bring happiness, though scripture permits self-defence against such aggressors.

verses.transliteration:

kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ mitradrohe ca pātakam

verses.translation: Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families, and no sin in hostility to friends,

verses.explanation: A new movement begins: we versus they. *They* cannot see — lobha-upahata-cetasaḥ, minds struck down by greed — but *we* see. Arjuna's diagnosis of the Kauravas is accurate; greed truly has eaten their judgment. The danger is subtler: the moment 'I see clearly and they are blind' becomes the premise, one's own blindness gets a place to hide. Arjuna's clarity about their delusion is itself entangled in his own.
verses.connection: Having closed his own case (1.37), he concedes the other side's greed-blinded sight, so as to set his own clear sight against it in the next verse.
verses.reflection: Others' blindness does not excuse yours; where you see clearly, you are the responsible one.
verses.background: Arjuna anticipates another reply: the Kauravas accept the sin of killing kin and fight anyway, so why not he? Śrīdhara takes this verse and the next as his answer, which begins here with the Kaurava leaders' state of mind.
verses.hook: What do the Kauravas fail to see because of their greed?

refs.note: Advises against quarrelling with priests, teachers, maternal uncles, elders and relatives, the very people Arjuna now faces in battle.

views.text: Answers the objection 'they face the same guilt of killing kin, so fight as they do': their discernment is wrecked by greed for kingdom, so they see no fault; we who see it must turn back.
Arjuna, by nature averse to needless violence, notes that greed blinds the Kauravas to the sin of destroying family and betraying friends.

kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ prapaśyadbhirjanārdana
verses.essence: — why should we, who clearly see the evil of destroying the family, not know to turn back from this sin?
verses.translation: Why should not we who clearly see evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (ought to be known)

anvaya.parts: कुल (family) + क्षय (destruction) + कृत (made, caused): caused by the family's destruction
