verses.explanation: The sentence completes: their blindness does not license ours. As ethics this is unimpeachable — wrong does not become right because the other side committed it first. The key verb is nivartitum, to turn back, to withdraw: the first explicit naming of retreat as the righteous act. Arjuna has now built a complete moral identity around leaving the field. What feels like conscience is also, conveniently, an exit.
verses.connection: Completes the sentence begun in 1.38: their blindness is set against 'we who clearly see', and the verdict of 1.37 becomes turning away from sin.
verses.reflection: Where you clearly see a wrong, ask what turning back from your own part in it would look like today.
verses.background: This verse completes the sentence Arjuna began in 1.38 about the Kauravas, blinded by greed. He turns from them to himself and his brothers, addressing Krishna as Janardana.
verses.hook: If the other side cannot see the sin, why should Arjuna commit it?

refs.note: Advises against quarrelling with priests, teachers, maternal uncles, elders and relatives, the very people Arjuna now faces in battle.

views.text: Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but knowing wrongdoing is worse: deliberate sinful conduct would be a grave crime, unworthy of those who see more clearly.
Arjuna argues that since he sees the evil of destroying a family, he should not repeat the Kauravas' sin when he can avoid it.

verses.devanagari:

verses.translation: In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety, indeed, overcomes the whole family.

कुल (family) + धर्म (duty, rite): the family's duties

verses.explanation: Arjuna's final argument is sociological, and it is serious: war kills the men who carry a family's traditions — its kula-dharma, the inherited grammar of rites, duties, restraints. Lose the carriers and the tradition dies with them; into that vacuum, adharma flows like water into a breached dam. He is describing what we would call the collapse of an institution's living memory. The cascade he now unrolls (1.40–44) is his most systematic case: not my grief, but civilization itself, forbids this war. By the social theory of his age every premise holds; the Gita will not refute the speech point by point, but change the frame in which it seems the only speech possible.
verses.connection: From personal grief (1.28–37) and comparative ethics (1.38–39), the argument now goes structural: what war does to the social order.
verses.reflection: Consider what traditions actually hold your people together — and which ones merely hold them still.
verses.background: Having concluded that he and his brothers should turn back, Arjuna gives Krishna his reasons in terms of the family. He starts a chain of consequences that runs through 1.44, beginning from the destruction of a family line.
verses.hook: What happens to a family's traditions when its elders are killed?

views.text: Notes that 'adharma overwhelms' names a fault of the mind; the next verse moves on to a fault of the body.
Takes dharma here concretely: the duties and ceremonies a family practises according to the injunctions of scripture.
Elders carry a family's values and customs; if they die early, the next generation loses guidance and drifts from the virtuous path, so Arjuna wants them spared.

verses.devanagari:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः ।

verses.transliteration:

strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṅkaraḥ
verses.essence: When adharma prevails, the family's women are corrupted; when women are corrupted, confusion of lineage is born.
verses.translation: By the prevalence of impiety, O Krishna, the women of the family become corrupt; and , women being corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), there arises intermingling of castes.

anvaya.parts: अधर्म (unrighteousness) + अभिभव (dominance): the prevailing of adharma
कुल (family) + स्त्री (woman): the family's women

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, locative plural (with दुष्टासु: 'when women…')
past participle, feminine, locative plural (when … are corrupted)

anvaya.parts: वर्ण (social class) + सङ्कर (mixing): mixture of classes

verses.explanation: The cascade continues in the idiom of Arjuna's age: with the men dead and order broken, the lineage system itself — varṇa-saṅkara, the 'mixing' his society most feared — unravels. Read him historically, not as a moral authority for today: he is voicing the deepest anxiety of an ancient patriarchal order, that war dissolves the very structures that tell people who they are. The Gita records this fear, and Krishna's first answer comes from another level entirely: the undying self of chapter 2, not the social order.
verses.connection: Step two of the cascade begun in 1.40: from broken dharma to broken lineage.
verses.reflection: When structures fail, the most vulnerable absorb the damage first. Ask who that is in your world.
verses.background: Arjuna's chain of consequences moves on, spoken to Krishna as Varshneya, 'descendant of Vrishni'. Śrīdhara counts the previous verse's harm as one of the mind and this one as a harm of the body.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna fear will happen to the women of a lawless family?

refs.note: Says the gods rejoice where women are honoured, supporting the view that a family's virtue depends on its women.

views.text: Reads praduṣyanti, the women's corruption, as the bodily fault that follows the mental fault named in the previous verse.
Arjuna fears that without elders to guide and protect, the family's women may be misled, children of mixed lineage born, and family traditions and rites for the ancestors lost.

verses.explanation: The cascade now reaches beyond the living: with no qualified descendants to offer piṇḍa and water, even the dead fall from their world. In Arjuna's cosmology the family is a vertical community — ancestors above, descendants below, the living as the link that feeds both directions. War, he argues, snaps the chain in the middle and the whole line, past and future, plummets together. It is the widest possible scope for the harm: this battle would damage eternity.
verses.connection: Step three of the cascade: the catastrophe of 1.41 propagates upward to the ancestors themselves.
verses.reflection: Notice how one broken link is never one: trace a single neglect outward through its generations.
verses.background: The next link in Arjuna's chain concerns the departed. In his world the ancestors depend on rice-balls and water offered by their descendants, so the confusion of lineage he has just named reaches back to them.
verses.hook: Where does Arjuna say confusion in the family leads, and for whom?

verses.explanation: The word utsādyante means torn up by the roots — what 1.40 called 'perishing' is now total extirpation. Arjuna's vocabulary insists on permanence lost: dharmas that are sanātana, śāśvata — eternal — destroyed by a single war. Notice the quiet contradiction he cannot see: if these laws are truly eternal, how can arrows abolish them? The tension between what is genuinely imperishable and what merely feels permanent is precisely where Krishna's answer will begin.

verses.reflection: What did your ancestors hand you that you are still feeding — and what have you let go hungry?

verses.hook: What do the family-destroyers' wrongs uproot, according to Arjuna?

verses.explanation: Arjuna seals his case with a citation: iti anuśuśruma, 'so have we heard' — the formula for received tradition. He is no longer arguing from feeling but from authority, the inherited word. It is the most honest moment of his lament: pressed to the edge of what he knows, he reaches for what he was told. The Gita will honor scripture but not stop there — Krishna will ask him, in effect, to move from what was heard to what can be known.
verses.connection: The cascade closes with an appeal to tradition's authority — the last brick in Arjuna's wall of reasons.
verses.reflection: Sit one minute with the worst-case story your mind tells, without arguing or obeying it.
verses.background: Arjuna's chain reaches its last point: the fate after death of men whose family rites have been lost. He speaks of it to Krishna, as Janardana, as something he has heard rather than reasoned out.
verses.hook: What fate has Arjuna heard awaits those who lose their family duties?

verses.explanation: The cry aho bata — alas! — and then a devastating self-inclusion: *we* are resolved, *our* greed. The accusation of 1.38 ('their minds corrupted by greed') has swung around and struck Arjuna himself. For one verse he sees no difference between the two armies: everyone on this field, himself included, has been bought. It is his bleakest and in some ways truest perception — and it leaves him nowhere at all to stand.
verses.connection: The 'we see / they are blind' division of 1.38–39 collapses: the greed he diagnosed in them he now confesses in himself.
verses.reflection: Catch yourself mid-rationalization today: the moment a noble reason arrives suspiciously on time.
verses.background: The argument about family ruin is complete and Arjuna's speech nears its end. He turns from consequences to the present moment, he and his brothers standing armed on the field, and cries out to Krishna.
verses.hook: What great sin does Arjuna think his side is about to commit?

views.text: Takes 'we' to mean everyone on the field, Kauravas and Pandavas alike; when all are undiscerning, Arjuna, who can still discern, concludes that the proper act is to turn back from battle.
Arjuna blames the coming sin on greed while missing his own weakness: his pity is attachment, not spiritual insight, and it makes him forget his warrior's duty.

verses.essence: Better for me if Dhritarashtra's armed sons killed me in battle — unresisting and unarmed.
verses.translation: If the sons of Dhritarashtra with weapons in hand should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + प्रतीकार (resistance): offering no resistance
अ (without) + शस्त्र (weapon): without weapons

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative plural (describes the sons)
anvaya.parts: शस्त्र (weapon) + पाणि (hand): those with weapons in hand

verses.explanation: The lament's last word is a death-wish dressed as ethics: let them kill me unarmed, that would be kṣemataram — 'safer', more secure. The comparative is haunting: safer than what? Than living with the guilt, than choosing at all. Arjuna has reasoned his way to preferring annihilation over action. When a chain of sincere arguments terminates in 'better that I cease', the flaw is rarely in the final step — it is in a premise buried far upstream. Finding that premise is what the remaining seventeen chapters are for.
verses.connection: The vow of 1.35 ('I would not kill even if killed') hardens into its extreme: actively preferring to be slain.
verses.reflection: There is a martyrdom that is really avoidance. Ask whether your surrender serves anyone at all.
verses.background: Arjuna's lament reaches its final words. With Dhritarashtra's sons standing armed across the field, he tells Krishna what outcome he would now prefer to the battle.
verses.hook: Why would Arjuna rather be killed unarmed than fight?

views.text: Presents this as Arjuna's step beyond merely turning back: having judged withdrawal proper, he declares it more proper still to be slain unresisting.
Arjuna's delusion reaches the point where he would let himself be killed unarmed, never seeing that leaving wrongdoers unpunished would harm society more.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः सङ्ख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् ।
विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः॥
verses.transliteration:
evamuktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśat
visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ
verses.essence: Having spoken thus, Arjuna sinks onto the chariot seat, casting away bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief.
verses.translation: Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna, casting away his bow and arrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot with his mind overwhelmed with sorrow.

anvaya.parts: रथ (chariot) + उपस्थ (seat, lap): the chariot's seat
स (with) + शर (arrow): along with the arrows
शोक (grief) + संविग्न (agitated) + मानस (mind): one whose mind is shaken with grief

verses.explanation: Sanjaya returns to close the chapter with a single image: the world's greatest archer sitting down on the seat of his chariot, bow and arrows dropped, mind shaken with śoka. He sinks down in the middle of the field — unable to advance, unwilling to retreat, paralyzed at the exact midpoint of his life's contradiction. Every argument has been made and nothing is resolved. The chapter is titled Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga: even this despair is called a yoga, because honest collapse is the doorway. Where a man can no longer move, he can finally listen.
verses.connection: Chapter 1 ends where 1.20 began: the bow Arjuna lifted is thrown down, and the trembling of 1.29–30 ends in collapse on the chariot seat.
verses.reflection: When you finally sink down, sink honestly. Collapse witnessed without disguise is where teaching begins.
verses.background: Sanjaya takes back the narrative to tell the king how Arjuna's speech ends. Śrīdhara reads Arjuna's refusals as total: even if the Kauravas are aggressors, even if retreat brings dishonour, even if Krishna himself urges him to fight.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna do after pouring out his grief to Krishna?

views.text: Has Arjuna throw down bow and arrow and sit on the chariot as if to fast to death, his refusal born of love, compassion and grief at the coming separation from his kin.
Glosses saṃvigna-mānasaḥ as one whose resolve to fight has been violently shaken, from the root vij, to fear and tremble; the bow and arrows are dropped like the ladles of the battle-sacrifice.
Arjuna, once the sage Nara and a devoted soul, collapses in grief; Krishna deliberately allowed this confusion so the Gita's teaching could be given for future generations.
